newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Austrian textiles fear wipeout, hit out at EU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Austrian textiles fear wipeout, hit out at EU.

text.p: Austria's textile and clothing industries, faced with mounting job losses and the risk of total wipeout, have attacked the European Union for subsidising textile sectors among competitors outside the EU.
EU cash support to eastern Europe and Turkey is hurting the textile industry throughout the bloc, Austrian textile producers say.
"The EU should not subsidise the textile industry in Turkey or eastern Europe," said Franz Pitnik, consultant at Austria's clothing industry association. "This is a vulnerable sector."

The number of employees in the Austrian textile industry has dropped by more than 30 percent to 21,500 in the last five years, while the clothing industry workforce has shrunk by more than 40 percent to 13,000.

"The EU should support areas which don't hurt EU companies, such as rail, hospital or telecommunication projects, but not our vulnerable sector. We don't need to boost the competition, which is growing fast enough as it is," Pitnik said.

The European Commission has recognised that the region's textile producers are struggling and earlier this month decided to include only token products in a second phase of textile liberalisation to come into effect next year.
Goods on the list -- ski suits, corsets and suspenders -- are not normally associated with the EU's trading partners in the developing world.
The move may ease textile producers' concerns about the future but it is unlikely to reverse damage suffered by the industry since the start of the decade.
In Austria between 1990 and 1995, annual production figures for textiles fell to 26 billion schillings ($2.41 billion) from 33 billion, and in the clothing industry to 10.4 billion from 14.7 billion.

In the textile sector, modern technology is also a main factor leading to job losses. But many in the clothing industry blame the decline on the transfer of wage-intensive production to cheaper foreign countries.
A customs agreement between the EU and Turkey, which came into effect on January 1 this year, will put further pressure on the European textile industry, industrialists say.
Within the EU there are about 2.3 million employees in the textile and clothing industry. According to EU estimates this number could drop by 850,000 by 2008.
The German textile industry employed 139,000 by the end of May, a drop from 143,000 in January.

A spokesman for the German Textile Industry Association said this sharp downward trend was likely to continue this year because of the weak German economy and competition from non-EU countries. In 1990, the industry employed 209,000.
Dionys Lehner, chief executive of Austria's Linz Textil AG, said Turkey planned to increase its textile exports to the EU by 150 percent to around $10 billion.
Turkey was not likely to reach that target this year but it was by far the greatest investor in the business, Lehner said.
"Their investments in the textile industry are probably as big as those of the whole EU-textile industry," he added.
Austria's textile and clothing industry associations have complained to the EU's textile industry association Euratex about the EU grants to non-EU countries in the sector.
Pitnik pinpointed projects in Turkey and Hungary, where the EU has subsidised nine companies through the PHARE-programme which provides technical aid to east European countries.
Those companies which previously used cheap labour for mass production are now subsidised by the EU to design their own collections and bring these to the market.

Wolfgang Zeyringer, consultant to the textile association said: "We aren't against investing in the infrastructure of these countries, if European companies could perhaps be involved in supplying the materials."

The aim now is to prevent follow-up projects. Pitnik knows he has the southern European countries, including Greece and Portugal on his side. Both cheap-labour countries, they would like to bring their own collections on to the market.
"We don't like the high-handed way EU officials just give away grants worth 20 to 30 million schillings", Pitnik said.
Linz Textil's Lehner agrees there is a lack of a clear economic policy within the EU. He believes the duty free deal with Turkey served political rather than economic interests.
"You get the feeling the EU is a political committee and an economic forum but without a clearly defined economic policy." ($1=10.77 Schilling)
